title: PlanningReady: South Australia (approval pathways)
notes: First sourced rules for South Australia, statewide. Built on 2026-10-12 from PlanSA pages, the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Fees Notice effective 1 July 2026, the Ancillary Accommodation Code Amendment and sa.gov.au. Every reference is UNVERIFIED and carries a summary, not the source's wording. Planning and Design Code zones, overlays and policies are not encoded.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Exempt development needs no approval (Schedules 4, 4A, 5 and 13 of the General Regulations 2017). Accepted development needs building consent only, no planning consent. Deemed-to-satisfy development is straightforward, envisaged for its location, fast-tracked and cannot be refused. Performance assessed development is assessed on merit against the Planning and Design Code and may involve public notification or referrals. Restricted development is assessed by the State Planning Commission. The Code online and the SA Property and Planning Atlas show the zones, overlays and likely pathways for a property. Accredited professionals can decide eligible applications.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Lodgement fee by development cost from $98.50 (up to $10,000) to $197 ($300,001 to $500,000) and more for larger projects. Deemed-to-satisfy planning consent $151 (under $10,000) or $250. Performance assessed $299 or 0.125% of cost up to $200,000, whichever is greater. Building consent Class 1 $538 or 0.25% of cost; Class 10 $154 or 0.25%. Certificate of Approval (land division certificate) $1,229. Certificate of Occupancy $59.50. Class 1 inspection $287. references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Ancillary accommodation is on the same site as an existing dwelling and ancillary to it, can be self-contained, and has no more than 2 bedrooms or rooms capable of being bedrooms. Deemed-to-satisfy criteria include a floor area of 70 m2 or less, wall height up to 3 m, roof height up to 5 m, not in front of the dwelling's building line, no separate connection to utilities and services, and unrestricted access to the existing dwelling's private open space. The amendment had interim operation from 29 February 2024.

rule_sets.title: South Australia: houses, extensions and granny flats
rule_sets.description: Planning consent, building consent and development approval in South Australia for new houses, extensions and ancillary accommodation.
limitations: We don't know your zone or the overlays on your land, so we can't say which assessment pathway applies, only which approvals you may need.
The Planning and Design Code's zone and overlay rules are not encoded. The free SA Property and Planning Atlas (SAPPA) shows your zone and overlays.
Constraints like heritage, bushfire and flooding come from your answers. Not ticking one doesn't mean it doesn't apply.
Not legal advice. Confirm with your council, an accredited professional or a town planner before you rely on it.

rules.title: Planning consent may be needed, depending on zone and overlays

outcomes.title: You may need planning consent
outcomes.detail: In South Australia the Planning and Design Code sets the pathway for your project. Minor work may be exempt or accepted (building consent only). A new house in a residential zone is often deemed-to-satisfy, which is decided in 5 business days and can't be refused if it meets every criterion. Anything else is performance assessed on merit, in 20 to 70 business days. Look up your zone and overlays on the SA Property and Planning Atlas (SAPPA).

approval.authority: Your local council (assessment manager or assessment panel), or an accredited professional for eligible deemed-to-satisfy applications
approval.pathway: Planning consent under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016, assessed against the Planning and Design Code

evidence.title: Site plan with setbacks, heights and existing buildings

payload.task: Look up your zone and overlays on SAPPA and check the pathway in the Planning and Design Code

rules.notes: MAY_APPLY because we don't know the zone or overlays.

outcomes.title: You likely need building consent
outcomes.detail: Building a house, granny flat or extension needs building consent, checked against the National Construction Code. Your council or a private building certifier (an accredited professional) can give it. For a house it takes 20 business days, plus 10 if referred to SCAP. The fee to council is $538 or 0.25% of the cost, whichever is greater.

approval.authority: Your council or an accredited professional (private building certifier)
approval.pathway: Building consent under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016, assessed against the Building Rules (National Construction Code)

payload.task: Choose your council or a private building certifier for building consent

rules.title: Development approval comes after all consents

outcomes.title: You need development approval before you start
outcomes.detail: Development approval is the final step. It is issued once every consent you need (planning, building and any land division) is granted. You can't start work until you have it. It is issued through the PlanSA portal.

approval.authority: Your local council or the State Planning Commission, once every consent is granted
approval.pathway: Development approval under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016

payload.task: Wait for development approval on the PlanSA portal before work starts

rules.title: Heritage places need planning consent

outcomes.title: Heritage listing means you likely need planning consent
outcomes.detail: If your property is a State Heritage Place or Local Heritage Place, or is in a Historic Area, the Code's heritage overlays apply. Work is usually performance assessed and State Heritage Places are referred to the state heritage authority. Expect longer timeframes (50 or 70 business days) and talk to your council early.

approval.authority: Your local council (assessment manager or assessment panel), or an accredited professional for eligible deemed-to-satisfy applications
approval.pathway: Planning consent under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016, assessed against the Planning and Design Code

payload.task: Check the heritage overlays for your land on SAPPA and talk to your council

rules.notes: Overlay names (State Heritage Place, Local Heritage Place, Historic Area) are from knowledge of the Code, not read this session.

rules.title: Bushfire hazard overlays add requirements

outcomes.title: A bushfire overlay may affect your design
outcomes.detail: Land in one of the Code's Hazards (Bushfire) overlays has extra planning rules, like access for fire trucks, water supply and vegetation clearance, and the building must be built to the right bushfire construction level. In higher risk areas the application may be referred to the CFS, which adds time. Check the overlay on SAPPA.

approval.authority: Your local council (assessment manager or assessment panel), or an accredited professional for eligible deemed-to-satisfy applications
approval.pathway: Planning consent under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016, assessed against the Planning and Design Code

payload.task: Check which Hazards (Bushfire) overlay applies on SAPPA

rules.notes: Overlay detail and CFS referral not read this session; WARNING outcome.

outcomes.title: Flooding may change your floor levels and pathway
outcomes.detail: If your land is in a flood hazard overlay, the Code can set minimum floor levels and other design rules. That can move your application from deemed-to-satisfy to performance assessed. Check the overlays on SAPPA and ask your council about flood levels.

payload.task: Check flood overlays on SAPPA and ask council for the flood level

rules.title: Trees and native vegetation

outcomes.title: Removing or damaging trees may need approval
outcomes.detail: Removing or damaging a regulated or significant tree is development in South Australia and needs approval. Clearing native vegetation can also need separate approval. Ask your council or an arborist before you plan to remove trees.

approval.authority: Your local council (assessment manager or assessment panel), or an accredited professional for eligible deemed-to-satisfy applications
approval.pathway: Planning consent under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016, assessed against the Planning and Design Code

evidence.title: Arborist report on trees on and near the site

payload.task: Ask council whether any tree on the site is regulated or significant

rules.notes: Regulated tree rules are from knowledge, not read this session.

rules.title: Houses don't need a certificate of occupancy

outcomes.title: No certificate of occupancy for a house or granny flat
outcomes.detail: A certificate of occupancy is needed for new habitable buildings in South Australia, except Class 1a buildings such as houses and granny flats. Your builder still has to finish the work in line with the approval, and inspections apply.

rule_sets.description: Ancillary accommodation rules in the Planning and Design Code.

rules.title: Granny flats up to 70 m2 can be deemed-to-satisfy

outcomes.title: At 70 m2 or less, your granny flat may be deemed-to-satisfy
outcomes.detail: Under the Planning and Design Code, ancillary accommodation up to 70 m2 can be deemed-to-satisfy if it also meets the other criteria: wall height up to 3 m, roof up to 5 m, not in front of the house, no separate utility connections and shared access to the backyard. Deemed-to-satisfy is decided in 5 business days and can't be refused. You still need planning and building consent.

approval.authority: Your local council (assessment manager or assessment panel), or an accredited professional for eligible deemed-to-satisfy applications
approval.pathway: Planning consent under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016, assessed against the Planning and Design Code (deemed-to-satisfy where every criterion is met)

payload.task: Check your design against the ancillary accommodation deemed-to-satisfy criteria

outcomes.title: Over 70 m2, your granny flat will likely be performance assessed
outcomes.detail: Ancillary accommodation over 70 m2 doesn't meet the deemed-to-satisfy floor area. It is likely to be performance assessed on merit, which takes 20 business days or more and can be refused.

approval.authority: Your local council (assessment manager or assessment panel), or an accredited professional for eligible deemed-to-satisfy applications
approval.pathway: Planning consent under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016, assessed against the Planning and Design Code (performance assessed)

payload.task: Ask a town planner whether a smaller design would be quicker

rules.notes: Ancillary Accommodation Code Amendment set 70 m2 (not 60 m2 as first proposed). Zone exclusions not confirmed.

rules.title: Ancillary accommodation has at most 2 bedrooms

outcomes.title: With more than 2 bedrooms it isn't ancillary accommodation
outcomes.detail: The Code defines ancillary accommodation as having no more than 2 bedrooms or rooms that could be bedrooms. With more, it is treated as a second dwelling, which is usually performance assessed and may not be allowed in your zone.

payload.task: Reduce to 2 bedrooms or get planning advice on a second dwelling

rules.title: Ancillary accommodation must go with an existing house

outcomes.title: Your granny flat would sit with your existing house
outcomes.detail: Ancillary accommodation must be on the same site as an existing dwelling and ancillary to it. You can rent it to anyone: approval conditions can't stop it being leased.

outcomes.title: Without a house on the site, it isn't ancillary accommodation
outcomes.detail: Ancillary accommodation has to be on the same site as an existing dwelling. If there is no house yet, apply for the house first or together, or get planning advice.

outcomes.title: You need land division consent and a land division certificate
outcomes.detail: Dividing land in South Australia needs development approval for the land division, usually lodged by a licensed surveyor on the PlanSA portal and assessed by SCAP or your council. Consent takes 30 business days for 10 or fewer lots with no new road, otherwise 60. Once conditions are met, you get a land division certificate ($1,229) and lodge the plan with Land Services SA for new titles.

approval.authority: State Commission Assessment Panel (SCAP) or your council, depending on the proposal
approval.pathway: Land division consent and a land division certificate (Certificate of Approval) under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016

evidence.title: Proposed plan of division from a licensed surveyor

payload.task: Engage a licensed surveyor to prepare and lodge the land division application

rules.title: Development approval for the land division

outcomes.title: Development approval follows land division consent
outcomes.detail: After land division consent (and any planning or building consent), development approval is issued. Then the conditions must be met before the land division certificate.

approval.authority: Your local council or the State Planning Commission, once every consent is granted
approval.pathway: Development approval under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016

rules.title: Open space contribution

outcomes.title: Budget for an open space contribution per new lot
outcomes.detail: Land divisions of 20 or fewer lots usually pay into the Planning and Development Fund instead of giving land for parks. From 1 July 2026 it is $10,166 for each new lot in Greater Adelaide and $3,723 elsewhere in South Australia. It is paid before the land division certificate is issued.

payload.task: Budget for the open space contribution for each new lot

outcomes.title: Larger land divisions must provide open space
outcomes.detail: Land divisions of more than 20 lots generally have to set aside at least 12.5% of the land for open space, or pay in lieu where allowed.

rules.notes: Payment timing (before the certificate) is from knowledge of section 198, not read this session.

outcomes.title: Bushfire overlays affect subdivision design
outcomes.detail: In a Hazards (Bushfire) overlay, new lots may need fire truck access, water supply and space for asset protection zones. Your surveyor and planner should design for this from the start.

rules.title: A change of use may need planning consent

outcomes.title: You may need planning consent for the new use
outcomes.detail: Changing how land or a building is used is development in South Australia. Whether it needs planning consent, and which pathway applies, depends on the zone and the new use in the Planning and Design Code. Check on SAPPA and the Code online, then ask your council.

rules.title: Building consent for a change of classification

outcomes.title: You may need building consent and a certificate of occupancy
outcomes.detail: If the new use changes the building's classification under the National Construction Code, or needs building work, you need building consent ($202 to change classification). A certificate of occupancy ($59.50) is needed before people use a new habitable building other than a house.

outcomes.title: You may need a certificate of occupancy
outcomes.detail: A certificate of occupancy is required for new habitable buildings other than Class 1a houses. If your change of use needs building consent, ask whether you need one before you open or move in.

approval.authority: Your council or the accredited professional who granted building consent

rules.title: Start with SAPPA and the Code

outcomes.title: Look up your zone and overlays on SAPPA
outcomes.detail: The SA Property and Planning Atlas (SAPPA) is free and shows your zone, subzone and overlays. Then check the rules in the Planning and Design Code online. Together they show whether your project is likely exempt, accepted, deemed-to-satisfy or performance assessed. Questions: PlanSA service desk on 1800 752 664.

payload.task: Look up your property on SAPPA

outcomes.title: You can use a private certifier
outcomes.detail: In South Australia, accredited professionals can decide eligible applications instead of council. A private building certifier can give building consent, and accredited planners can decide some deemed-to-satisfy planning applications. They set their own fees.

outcomes.title: Your project may need development approval
outcomes.detail: Some minor work is exempt (like many fences and small sheds) and some is accepted, needing building consent only (like many carports). We can't tell from the description. Check the Code and SAPPA, and ask your council.
